pr_title: Fix looking at with 180 degree arc
pr_body:
- Supersedes/closes https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/93653
- Fixes https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/80249
- Fixes https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/57457
- Fixes https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/53793

Have it calculate the perpendicular vectors by the cross product of the constants vector3 `(1, 0, 0)` or `(0, 1, 0)` depends on the nearest axis and implement the similar[^1] approach as #93653 in a more simple way. Also, for `looking_at()` and `look_at()`, allow this with a warning (and explain it in the document).

[^1]: This PR may cause a breaking compatibility in that the quaternion of the 180 degree rotation will be inverted for consistency in the direction of rotation, but this is almost never a problem unless you use slerp, etc. in the special situation of generating a 180 degree arc. If you really want to migrate/make compatibility it, the user can align the phase of the quaternion, as in `Quaternion(Basis(Quaternion(v0, v1)))`.
pr_comments: We tend to require more help with documentation!
Realised I have confused this function with another (probably relative rotation), sorry for wall of text and confusion.

Could using the current `Basis` as the "previous value" you refer to be an acceptable middle ground ?

Wouldn't solve all 3 cases you mention but at least provide consistent results in the FPS case where the `Basis` is updated incrementally.

> Could using the current Basis as the "previous value" you refer to be an acceptable middle ground ?

For the `Node` at least, deriving `previous_yaw` from the existing basis would be a first step, but it is still susceptible to problems with (2), although as I say in the case close to `p_up` (or 180) it could simply not alter the basis at all (in which case the yaw would be preserved).

For `Basis` itself, it would be strictly speaking breaking compatibility as it would be relying on the current contents (although maybe this doesn't matter too much as previous behaviour is so broken). Also the case for (2) would have to be handled.

(Incidentally, I've not done or planning any PRs on this, am happy to review any more in depth fixes based on the above.)

_BTW there's an extra situation to deal with which is the flipping (or not) of yaw when you cross the up vector. But that's an implementation detail._

In my thinking, the definition of the current yaw is ambiguous for Basis and Quaternion, so there is not much point in worrying about it. Although I feel that it is not correct in the first place that z-axis has a special meaning on the looking_at in Basis; If we want to solve that problem at Basis, I think not only previous_yaw but also forward_axis needs to be explicit, discontinuing the use_model_front parameter as well.

For Node3D, however, the current direction is explicit, so in cases 1 and 2, a preliminary check before calling Basis.looking_at() could improve things before the warning in Basis is reached; For case 2, we can do not to rotate. Since the user has no control over the very small vectors that would introduce errors, it is better to do nothing than to make a rotation that depends on it. However, there should be nothing that can be done about case 3, i.e., the 180-degree rotation case.

Also, this may be a niche case, but in cases where `looking_at()` is used to align yaw, it is necessary to be aware of the possibility that `looking_at()` may cause problems if the rotation is implicitly dependent on the previous yaw.

For example, if the bone orientation of a model loaded from an external source is used as it is, or if the orientation is different for each saved scene, there will be cases where the X and Y-axis will not match when `looking_at()` is used to match the rotation. Conversely, current this PR should result in the same X and Y-axis, although cause unintended rotation in Z-axis.

Given this, it appears that a warning is still required. In other words, since this needs to be handled by the user, I think a currently possible compromise is to provide a method for checking colinear case such as `Vector3.is_cololinear()` method and to write in the documentation how to prevent rotation with `looking_at()` on the user side; As similer idea with @lawnjelly said above:

> Another option to solve (2) is to not change the basis (as it is very close to up vector anyway), not report an error, but maybe return a false for success (in case the user wanted to act upon this).

Actually I wrote all that, but I think I was getting my wires crossed on a previous similar issue (it was from 3 years ago :grin: ), and I'm not super familiar with this function in Godot sorry for any confusion. :blush:

In the process of rebasing https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/87440, it is my understanding that the following is particularly misleading?

> The [param target] and the [param up] cannot be [constant Vector3.ZERO], and shouldn't be colinear to avoid unintended rotation around local Z axis.

First of all, it's "_collinear_".
Second, from what I can see, the original sentence was fine, as this is just a more mathematical way of saying "parallel to one other (regardless of direction)". There's little mentions of collinearity across all of Godot and doing it here makes it look more complicated than it is in practice.
Third, it's wrong, I think? `target` is a position vector and `up` is a direction vector. The **Node3D** version of the same method got this right:
> "and the direction from the node's position to the [param target] vector cannot be parallel to the [param up] vector."

Probably someone fixed this in the past, but it was not fixed in the other descriptions. This PR homogenised the inaccurate description.

@Mickeon Correct, so for the Basis method, it makes more sense say the direction from the origin to the target should not be parallel to the up vector. That way we are talking about these vectors as both being lines, and we talk about them being parallel. The word collinear implies working with points, but 2 points always form a line.

issue_context.title: `new Quaternion(Up, Down) * Up == Up`, but it should be Down
comments: What are you basing what it should be on? The other results flipping the vector?

Based on the description in the documentation, I assumed when an arc on a sphere goes from one side to the other, it should be a 180° rotation.
Moreover `new Quaternion(new Vector3(0.01f, 0.99f, 0).Normalized(), Vector3.Down).Normalized() * Vector3.Up`, gives `(0.010114331, -0.99994874, 0)` (so almost Down), which seems consistent with what I'd expect it to do. I will admit, however, I'm not very knowledgeable about the workings of quaternions and I might simply be misunderstanding what the function is supposed to do.

For any case where the two vectors are opposite it gives the quaternion `(0, 1, 0, 0)`, which flips through the Y-axis, the case with the vectors being up/down it might break down, but unsure how to handle that seemingly degenerate case
Again I don't know much about quaternions, but I'd guess flipping either the x-axis or the z-axis would work fine, as long as it's a 180° rotation.

Yes but how do you pick that? I'm not sure this particular use of this constructor is reliable, but I'm not fully familiar with the system

The method for constructing it breaks down when the vectors are parallel, which requires to just pick some value instead
As far as I can tell there's infinitely many possibilities for the shortest arc between the top and the bottom, so any arbitrary result is fine as long as it's one of the valid results.
But again, how to decide when this is the case? I think this should be documented as I suspect it's quite complex to try to add tests for this specific case

I believe if the exterior product (`a.X * b.Y - a.Y * b.X`) of two vectors is 0, they are collinear (by which I mean: facing the same direction or the opposite directions — but I'm not a mathematician so I might be using the wrong word here). I'm not sure how to decide on a result in the general case though.

We check it by seeing if the two vectors are parallel and opposite, tested with the scalar product

My question is: Is this case degenerate? I'd suspect it is and it's not well defined, and the question is if it is worth it to ensure it gives one of the "valid" cases or just return a degenerate case (being clarified in the documentation of course)

Note that it also breaks down in a number of other cases when the input vectors are not along the axes, so that's much more complicated

For example, how would you pick the result for the input vector: `Vector3(1, 1, 1).normalized()` and the opposite of the same?
180 degree rotation around what axis though?

I think any axis should do, as long as it's the right kind of 180° rotation. Again there's infinitely many right answers in this situation, and as long as it's any of those, it seems to me that it should be okay.
But how do you find it?
It seems to me that any axis that is orthogonal to the two given parallel vectors would be okay, so you could use a cross product to find it.
That is true, the question is if it is worth the several added operations to find this since it is still undefined, there's no such thing as the "shortest arc" in this case

I thought you said the engine already checks for the case in which the vectors are parallel, in which case it seems to me this isn't really adding any further overhead except in the edge case where the vectors are indeed parallel — and that's the specific case that (in my opinion) currently isn't being handled particularly well. I don't really see any significant performance downside.

Well you'll have two, possibly three, cross products, and an normalization, which is quite a lot more

In total:
* 13 multiplications
* 3 comparisons (for checking if the first cross product is zero)
* One square root

But it seems to me the added operations would specifically only be in the code branch of the parallel edge case (which doesn't work all that well), and wouldn't affect the normal cases. I might be misunderstanding, though.

It won't, but that doesn't remove the performance increase here

I think there needs to be some argument in favor of this case being a case that isn't degenerate and is worth actually finding a universal fix for

It's really in my opinion a question of finding a less wrong answer

I think taking a little extra time to produce a good result beats getting a wrong result very quickly.

Edit: I'll await further opinions, nevertheless thank you for your time, especially since it's a volunteer position.

Check if input vectors a, b are antiparallel, which is trivial if you check for parallel already.

If true create a vector which is guaranteed not to be parallel:
c = (abs(a.z)+1, a.x, a.y) would work for example.

Compute rotation axis:
r = normalize(cross(a, c))

Create 180 deg quaternion:
q = (0, r.x, r.y, r.z)

For me this is clearly a bug. The `from`, `to` arguments being the opposite vectors case is already being properly detected[^1], but the always returned 180 rotation around the Y-axis for such cases is correct only for cases when `from.y` is zero (`to.y` is also zero then).

If this constructor wouldn't be supposed to handle the opposite vectors then it shouldn't handle them in any way whatsoever. In such case documenting such unsupported behavior and erroring in every such case could be a solution. But as mentioned, this constructor already handles such cases, just most of them incorrectly.

Hence I think for the opposite vectors the proper thing to do is to make this constructor return a rotation by 180 around any arbitrarily choosen axis orthogonal to the input vectors. And document it clearly; users can always manually handle such case if some specific behavior is desired.
Likely makes sense to prefer returning rotation around Y axis (when it's correct), this would not change the behavior for the cases already working correctly.

Also looking at the code it seems like it assumes the input vectors are normalized (then dot product is equivalent to the cosine of the angle between the vectors), but it's not ensured/checked anyhow. This should be changed too.
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/16a93563bfd3b02ca0a8f6df2026f3a3217f5571/core/math/quaternion.h#L146-L148

[^1]: Given the input vectors are indeed normalized.

Documentation does not say anything about the case of opposite vectors returning unexpected results, and since a valid 180-degree rotation is still possible around an arbitrarily chosen axis, why don't just return that? With a note, that slerp-ing such rotation might yield unexpected results, since the axis is chosen at random.
That was more or less the consensus so far (minus the note kleonc made about preferring rotation around the Y axis). It's really just that no one has implemented a fix yet.
No offence taken, thank you for taking the time to clarify!

> @krisutofu I took some time this afternoon to implement your code. I should note that my understanding of the inner workings of quaternions is pretty limited but it doesn't seem like anyone else was going to do it. In general it went well except for one assertion I added to the test cases:
> 
> ```c++
> Vector3 left(-1, 0, 0);
> Vector3 right(1, 0, 0);
> Quaternion left_to_right(left, right);
> 
> // When the two vectors lie on the XZ plane, the rotation axis should be the
> // Y-axis for backwards compatibility.
> Vector3 left_to_right_axis = left_to_right.get_axis();
> CHECK(left_to_right_axis.abs().is_equal_approx(up));
> ```
> 
> As kleonc mentioned, when the parameter vectors are on the XZ plane, the resulting quaternion should rotate on the XZ plane because that's consistent with what the old code does. I briefly tried messing around with the code but I figured it's probably better to just ask. Could you let me know how I could adjust the code so that it stays backward compatible?
> 
> Currently `left_to_right` rotates on the XY plane (so around the Z-axis).
> 
> @AThousandShips It's very late but I was reading through the thread this morning and I'd like to apologize for the phrasing "since it's a volunteer position and all" because it sounded pretty dismissive when I read it back. I'm not great at social things and my intuition for which tone a text I'm writing has is occasionally pretty bad, but I had always meant this in the sense of "especially since it's a volunteer position." I really didn't mean to be ungrateful. Sorry for that!

Great 😊 . Sorry for my response latency. It went into email Spam. The change you need is quite simple, it only needs to swap two things. I assumed X -> Y -> Z order but you'd like to have X -> Z -> Y order.

Therefore the change is to swap these two lines:
```c++
		|| set_perpendicular_to(v0.y, v0.z, v0.x, y, z, x)
		|| set_perpendicular_to(v0.z, v0.x, v0.y, z, x, y);
```

to

```c++
		|| set_perpendicular_to(v0.z, v0.x, v0.y, z, x, y)
		|| set_perpendicular_to(v0.y, v0.z, v0.x, y, z, x);
```

XZ has a positive normal that faces downwards (-Y), given that X precedes Z (as it is implemented in the vector comparison). Therefore it gives a -Y as rotation axis (when v0 is Right and v1 is Left). If you still need that to be Y instead of -Y, you can swap the minus sign in the helper function which then gives the negated cross product.

With negated normal, it looks like this:

```c++
		out_y = in_z / length;
		out_z = -in_y / length;
```

Thank you for taking the time for the implementation. We will be grateful.

EDIT: If it relieves you, it's not just you. My communication and social skills are bad in my experience. It takes me a lot of time to find more precise natural language expressions and sometimes I am overthinking (emotionally and such and this makes me hide). As non-native speaker I may notice my phrasing issues less often. But, we are always seeking the benefit of the community, that's the good thing.

@krisutofu I thought your reply was plenty fast, there's really no need to apologize. I'm not sure if flipping the axis makes a significant difference, both directions seem to work equally well, but based on the old code I guessed that it used to always give a +Y rotation axis, so I've nevertheless added the change for flipping the axis. Thank you for the code and the kind words!

review_comments:
This might spam a lot, shouldn't it be `WARN_PRINT_ONCE`?

In general this kind of warnings aren't super helpful to end users, as a basis may end up in this state from internal engine code or complex calculations, and the warning doesn't point at which basis / object transform is referred to. So I'm not convinced this will make end users happy.

If look_at is called continuously, it may be spammed, but in that case it should not be called continuously in the first place, so spamming it is not considered excessive.

As mentioned in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/100991#issuecomment-2569178136, if the orientation is nearly the same, the user should detect it and do nothing. Well, this could be add documentation or changing a warning text.
Letting the user decide whether to normalize would make this function a little bit more generic and may allow optimizations down the road.

Gave it a second thought and I'm not sure this deserves to be a member function. It's definition is quite tricky to document clearly : it's supposed to return _some_ perpendicular vector. I'd suggest to make it rather a free function on the cpp.

Since Vector3 is a Godot-defined class, it could be a static function, but I think it would not make sense to define a function that returns some Vector3 outside of it. Also, if we expose this method to GDScript along with the documentation that "it returns some perpendicular vector", some users possibly always use this to get look_at up vectors, but that is never recommended, so I would keep this private.

If forced to document, it may become `Return the perpendicular vector by cross product with the Vector3.RIGHT or Vector3.UP, whichever has the greater angle to the current vector with the sign of each element positive.`

Well, honestly I do not prefer to document and publish this as an exact definition. The only essence is "to avoid being parallel to the current vector", and there is no mathematical basis for using `Vector3.RIGHT` and `Vector3.UP`, since it could be a different vector depending on the prior branching code `Math::abs(x) <= Math::abs(y) && Math::abs(x) <= Math::abs(z)`, although I believe it makes sense to use any of the axis of the basis due to the simplicity of the calculation process.

For now, I left it only in the comments so that later people will not be confused.

Also, I found in the Plane class has get_any_perpendicular_normal() as a non-exposed (to GDScript) member function, so I think it is okay to not make it public. BTW, I assume we should change the internal of get_any_perpendicular_normal() to use Vector3.perpendicular() as well, but it would be fine to make it a separate PR later as a follow up.
Maybe rename it to `get_any_perpendicular()` instead of just `perpendicular()` then.
